title: Longing for Belonging
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: An Australian educator examines why student belonging surveys in public schools consistently reveal disconnection and argues that popular school initiatives aimed at building belonging are fundamentally ineffective. The author surveys five common approaches -- fundraising embarrassments, free BBQs, pastoral care classes, themed cause days, and reward systems -- and shows each fails because it is tokenistic, disconnected from students' actual interests, or actively counterproductive. By contrast, the author's experiences in American and independent Australian schools reveal that genuine belonging emerges only when extracurricular participation is structurally embedded in the school day, making every student feel pride, connection, and daily success. The public school system's inability to codify this in teacher conditions leaves belonging as a goal endlessly chased with gestures that change nothing. The article concludes that high-quality teaching and consistent high expectations are the most effective belonging strategy available: students connect with places that make them feel safe and capable.
points: Token gestures like fundraising stunts and free BBQs fail to build belonging because they require no student investment and produce no lasting identity or pride in the school community.
Themed cause days and one-off events can actually heighten division by highlighting difference in isolation, without the continuous community context that makes difference a strength.

The critical design feature that independent and American schools get right is mandatory extracurricular participation -- students compete, achieve, and celebrate together daily, making school identity inseparable from personal identity.

Public school teachers already work through breaks and evenings; until the system pays them to run extracurriculars as a codified part of the job, belonging programs will always depend on teachers' altruism and will be insufficient.

The author's most counterintuitive claim: teaching well IS the belonging strategy. Students connect with schools where they feel academically safe and capable, not with schools that perform inclusivity through events.
quotes: In my experience within a few schools in my career, this data has almost always highlighted one thing strongly in the high school students I have chosen to work with. They do not have a connection to school. They do not feel a sense of belonging. School is just a place they go because they have to.
In its simplest form, belonging is the feeling of being accepted and valued in a community. A place where you can be your unfiltered self without a fear of judgement or exclusion.

Raising money for charity is a noble and important mission. We see it often that individuals will raise money for a cause they care deeply about and they incentivize their community by putting themselves through a challenge or great discomfort. In schools however, the money raised is rarely connected with the cause it's going towards.

Rewards are inherently flawed. They make the behaviour more about the outcome than the reason it is required. They can create superficial short term compliance based on extrinsic motivation which only exists as long as the reward is present.

These days are all well meaning but when we only give 24 hours (which is really 6 hours) to celebrate something it reeks of tokenism. One-offs do not create connection or community. Sometimes they can actually further highlight our differences and further increase any divide that exists.

This made me wonder, 'why on earth would a teenager proudly wear school branded clothing when it is completely optional'. The answer was that school wasn't just a place they came to learn, it was an all encompassing community where their hobbies and interests were built into the school day through sporting teams and clubs. This meant that every student was feeling some level of pride, connection and success every single day without it feeling like a hokey or forced addition.

I do not know a single teacher who does not want to make the students in front of them feel like they belong. But until the public system can codify this in their wages and conditions in a way that's sustainable then I believe that student belonging will continue to be a dragon that school leaders chase with tokenistic rituals and wonder why nothing changes.

At the end of the day the best strategy for improving student belonging within a school is consistent and high expectations for managing student behaviour and high quality teaching practice such as explicit teaching. Teaching well is the best wellbeing strategy. Students will connect with a place that makes them feel safe and capable.
